blocks.text: Prevest DenPro makes dental consumables: restorative materials, endodontic products, prosthetic materials, orthodontic products, preventive care products and some dental equipment [F] (AR2026 p.4). It has a portfolio of more than 100 products and sells in more than 90 countries [F] (PPT Jul 2026). Everything is made at one plant in the Export Promotion Industrial Park, Kartholi, Samba (Jammu & Kashmir), with stated installed capacity of more than 200 MT per annum [F] (AR2026 p.19). The company makes money by selling small, repeat-purchase consumables to dealers and distributors, who sell on to dentists, clinics and labs. Management says it does not supply most products directly to dentists [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). It also does some private-label and OEM manufacturing. Management claims it is currently an OEM supplier to 3 or 4 large companies, none of which are named [MC] (CALL Jul 2026).

**End markets and geography.** The company reports a single segment, so no product-line revenue or margin split is disclosed [F] (AR2026 p.73). The only audited revenue split is export versus domestic. In FY26 consolidated export sales were Rs 42.23 cr and domestic sales Rs 30.76 cr [F] (AR2026 p.80). That is about 57.9% export and 42.1% domestic on gross product sales [E] (AR2026 p.80). The annual report gives a continent split of 68.40% Asia, 14.98% Europe, 12.43% Africa, 2.31% South America, 1.77% North America and 0.11% Australia [F] (AR2026 p.9). It does not say whether the Asia figure includes India; we assume it does [AI]. The customer profile is a dealer network: management says 145+ dealers in India and 120+ overseas business partners [MC] (PPT Jul 2026). Customer concentration is not disclosed.

**Scale.** In FY26 our statements data shows revenue of Rs 72 cr, EBITDA of Rs 25 cr (35% margin), PAT of Rs 20 cr, zero borrowings and equity of Rs 125 cr [F] (NUMBERS). In Q1 FY27 (Jun 2026) sales were Rs 19.07 cr, up 20.9% YoY, and PAT was Rs 5.64 cr, up 27.9% YoY [F] (NUMBERS). At 31 March 2026 consolidated cash and bank balances were Rs 72.85 cr [F] (AR2026 p.77). That is about 55% of total assets of Rs 133.19 cr [E] (AR2026 p.77).

Listing status: the shares are listed on the SME Platform of BSE (scrip 543363). The company listed in 2021 and was still on the SME platform at the FY26 Board report [F] (AR2026 p.5, p.50). As an SME-listed company it is exempt from several corporate-governance regulations, including Regulations 17-27 [F] (AR2026 p.47). Its own commentary is half-yearly. Our evidence base has three years of annual statements, not ten [F] (NUMBERS). We had no prospectus or offer document, and no Q1 FY27 results commentary or transcript. The most recent call (29 June 2026) covered FY26 [F] (CALL Jul 2026).

blocks.text: Driver classification [AI]: theses 1 and 6 are structural (product economics and balance sheet). Theses 2, 4 and 5 are company-specific, depending on execution, distribution and brand building. Theses 3 and 7 are partly cyclical, because exports depend on forex availability, wars and tariffs in customer countries.

subsections.title: Bear thesis: reasons not to own it

items: 1. **The price needs growth the company has never delivered.** The reverse DCF implies about 37.1% annual sales growth for five years. The base case equivalent is 7.1% [E] (NUMBERS). Sales grew at about 13.4% a year from FY24 to FY26 [E] (NUMBERS). Even management's own target of crossing Rs 100 cr within three years [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) implies only about 11.7% a year [E].

2. **Management keeps missing its guidance.** It guided 30% growth for FY25 [MC] (CALL Nov 2024); FY25 sales grew about 12.5% on our statements data [E] (NUMBERS), and management itself put it at 13% [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). It guided that H2 FY26 growth would 'definitely' cross 20% [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); H2 FY26 consolidated revenue grew 11.97% [F] (PPT Jul 2026). Management also targeted Rs 20 cr of Oradox revenue in three years [MC] (CALL Nov 2024). Oradox sales were about Rs 0.5 cr in FY25 [MC] (CALL Jun 2025) and fell 2% in FY26 [MC] (CALL Jul 2026).

3. **Part of reported 'EBITDA' is treasury income.** Management's FY26 EBITDA of Rs 29.62 cr (38.6%) [MC] (CALL Jul 2026) includes other income. Our statements data shows operating EBITDA of Rs 25 cr (35%) [F] (NUMBERS). Interest on bank deposits was Rs 4.30 cr [F] (AR2026 p.80), and other income was 17.9% of PBT in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS).

4. **Working capital is getting worse.** Inventory days rose from 168 to 214 to 239 across FY24-FY26, and the cash conversion cycle from 189 to 229 days [F] (NUMBERS). Over three years CFO was only 0.78x PAT [F] (NUMBERS).

5. **There are governance lapses.** The secretarial auditor found that the company paid an executive director above the Section 197 limits without the required approvals. It also failed to make, or delayed, required Regulation 30 intimations [F] (AR2026 p.52). Shareholders were asked to waive recovery of Rs 11.38 lakh of excess pay [F] (AR2026 p.58). The statutory auditor's report says director remuneration complied with Section 197 [F] (AR2026 p.92). The two documents are not reconciled.

6. **Promoter-family pay is large relative to profit.** FY26 director remuneration was Rs 4.59 cr [F] (AR2026 p.80), about 22% of consolidated PAT [E]. The MD and WTD each take Rs 1.425 cr and the son-in-law CMO Rs 1.36 cr [F] (AR2026 p.46, p.63). The WTD's cap is proposed to rise to Rs 1.80 cr [F] (AR2026 p.63).

7. **Foreign subsidiaries are unaudited and the US claims are unverifiable.** The foreign subsidiaries' accounts were certified by management, not audited. Axiodent recorded revenue of Rs 12.63 lakh and negative net assets [F] (AR2026 p.96), and a loss of Rs 76.91 lakh [F] (AR2026 p.84). Management nonetheless claims US business grew 37.58% [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). North America is only 1.77% of revenue [F] (AR2026 p.9).

8. **All production sits on one site in a sensitive region.** There is one plant in Samba, J&K [F] (AR2026 p.19). Near-war conditions in Jammu stopped operations for about 10 days, and floods for another 10-15 days, in Q1 FY26 [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

9. **Dependence on imported inputs is rising.** Imported raw material purchases rose to Rs 11.55 cr from Rs 8.88 cr [F] (AR2026 p.70). That lifted the import share of purchases from about 57.9% to 63.7% [E], despite the import-substitution narrative.

10. **There is key-man and succession risk.** The founder-chairman is 72 [F] (AR2026 p.46). The FY26 results call was cancelled because of his medical emergency [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). The FY26 operating team consists of family members and a small group of executives [F] (AR2026 p.63).

**Is the DCF too harsh?** Possibly [AI]. Our DCF starts base-case growth at 4.2%. That is the TTM-versus-FY26 increment, not an annual growth rate [F] (NUMBERS). The model's equity value also equals EV minus borrowings, so it does not add the Rs 72.85 cr cash balance [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.77). Both choices push fair value down. Even the bull case (Rs 179.3) is 52.4% below the price [F] (NUMBERS), so the direction of the conclusion is unlikely to change [AI].

**Is margin quality better or worse than headline?** Management quotes 38.6% EBITDA [MC] (CALL Jul 2026); operating EBITDA is 35% [F] (NUMBERS). The 35% has held for three years despite inflation [F] (NUMBERS), and the gross margin proxy is high [E] (AR2026 p.85). Both the bull and bear readings have support.

**Is the new-vertical story real?** The verticals exist commercially: printers sold since November 2025 and the disinfectants commercialised [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). But no vertical revenue is disclosed. The only quantified data points are around Rs 0.5 cr each for Oradox and 3D resins in FY25 [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). The market may be paying for optionality that does not yet show in the numbers [AI].

**Is the stock cheap after a 33% fall from the high?** The price is 32.7% below the 52-week high of Rs 560 [F] (NUMBERS). It is still at 20.6x trailing P/E and 17.4x EV/EBITDA [F] (NUMBERS). With fewer than 2,000 shareholders [F] (NUMBERS), price discovery is thin [AI].

**Is the Q1 FY27 acceleration durable?** The +20.9% YoY in Q1 FY27 [F] (NUMBERS) compares against a quarter hit by near-war conditions, floods and GST disruption [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Part of the growth is base effect [AI].

blocks.text: Our view [AI] is that the market treats Prevest as a scarce, debt-free 'Indian dental MNC in the making' and prices growth the company has never produced. The more defensible view is a well-run, high-margin, export-led niche manufacturer growing in the low teens [F] (NUMBERS). It holds cash and mutual funds worth about 18% of its market capitalisation [E] (AR2026 p.77, p.79; NUMBERS), and the cash earns deposit rates. Its governance and disclosure fall short of what a 20x P/E multiple usually assumes. Where we may be too negative: the core business earns very high returns once cash is stripped out, at roughly 53% pre-tax on operating capital [E] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.77, p.79). If the Q1 FY27 pace holds and one new vertical scales, the growth gap could narrow faster than our DCF assumes [AI].

blocks.text: Promoter-linked entities outside the listed group are Dentstal India, a partnership of Atul and Namrata Modi, and NV International, a partnership of Atul and Niharika Modi [F] (AR2026 p.82). The scanned annual report text does not legibly disclose transaction amounts with them. The Board says there were no material related-party transactions [F] (AR2026 p.56). The consolidation note lists the UAE entity at 0% shareholding [F] (AR2026 p.89), although the Board report calls it wholly owned [F] (AR2026 p.46).

The core dental-materials business is about 25 years old [F] (AR2026 p.5). Nearly everything in the growth narrative is three years old or less: Oradox (2023), 3D resins and printers (2024), disinfectants and Rotoflex (2025), Axiodent (2025) and the UAE entity (2025-26) [F] (AR2026 p.8, p.51). So the earnings base is the legacy materials franchise, and the new lines have no meaningful revenue record [AI]. In Jun 2025 the MD said core products drove that year's growth and 'revenue from our diversified products is not very significant' [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). The board and company secretary were largely replaced in March-May 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.47-48), so the oversight structure is also new [AI].

items: 1. **R&D and formulation.** The in-house Prevest Research Institute is DSIR-recognised [F] (AR2026 p.41). It develops formulations and import-substitute raw materials such as MTA, hydroxyapatite, beta-TCP, bioglass, 10-MDP and N-benzoyl thiourea [F] (AR2026 p.41).

2. **Regulatory approvals.** The company holds ISO 13485:2016, CE, USFDA clearances for cements, cavity liners and root canal sealers, MDSAP, Saudi FDA and CDSCO MDR registrations [F] (AR2026 p.20-21).
3. **Raw material procurement.** FY26 purchases were Rs 19.47 cr, of which Rs 11.55 cr was imported and Rs 6.57 cr indigenous [F] (AR2026 p.70).
4. **Manufacturing.** A single GMP facility at EPIP Kartholi, with more than 200 MT per annum installed capacity [F] (AR2026 p.19), on a 60,000 sq ft site [MC] (PPT Jul 2026).
5. **Quality control and post-market surveillance** in in-house laboratories [MC] (AR2026 p.21).

6. **Distribution.** In India, products go through dealers, the Prevest Direct e-commerce site, conferences and marketplaces. Abroad they go through distributors, OEM/private label and Axiodent in the US [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Nov 2024; CALL Jun 2025).
7. **Demand creation.** Exhibitions, clinical education (about 16 programmes in FY26) and the IDA partnership [F] (AR2026 p.22) [MC] (CALL Jul 2026).

blocks.text: Value is captured mainly at the formulation and manufacturing stage. The gross margin proxy (revenue less material cost) was about 76.9% in FY26 and 78.3% in FY25 [E] (AR2026 p.85). The company's costs are mostly people (Rs 13.24 cr), freight, promotion and travel [F] (AR2026 p.80-81), not materials. Dental consumables are low-ticket items where the dentist's habit and trust matter more than price [AI]. Management claims a cost edge from Indian production and import duties [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). The weak point is brand. The MD said 'we cannot compete with those multinational companies' on brand [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), and US dentists disliked the 'made in India' label [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). That suggests part of the value chain, namely brand and end-customer pricing, is captured by distributors and OEM customers rather than by the company [AI].

The model is asset-light for a manufacturer. Net fixed assets have been flat at Rs 27 cr for three years, CWIP was zero, and capex was Rs 2-4 cr a year (2.8-7.1% of sales) [F] (NUMBERS). Fixed-asset turnover rose from 2.07x to 2.67x [F] (NUMBERS). Most of the capital is cash and working capital, not plant [E] (AR2026 p.77). The company outsources no manufacturing that we can find, but it relies on third parties for distribution [MC] (CALL Jun 2025).

blocks.text: Our read [AI]: the differentiated lines are the bioceramic and MTA endodontic materials and the specialised restoratives. The company makes some of the inputs in-house [F] (AR2026 p.41), and dentists tend to stay with a sealer or restorative they trust. Disinfectants, Oradox consumer products and private-label work look more commodity-like: low switching costs, many competitors, and channels (pharmacy, FMCG) where the company has no record. Management says the top 20 products give 55% of revenue, and in the same answer says 60% [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Either way, the core range carries the business.

The company reports one segment: manufacturing and marketing of dental materials and allied products [F] (AR2026 p.44, p.73). It does not disclose segment margins [F] (AR2026 p.73). The only audited split is export versus domestic, shown below. The FY24 split is our estimate, back-solved from management's FY25 growth rates.

items: **Exports, +18.0% FY26.** Management attributes this to markets coming out of forex crises and to shifting sales to other countries [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Jul 2026). Our read [AI]: this is mostly cyclical recovery from a flat FY24, and it slowed sharply to +3.56% in H2 versus H1 [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). Q4 was hit by war-related shipping disruption [MC] (CALL Jul 2026).

**Domestic, +9.0% FY26.** H1 suffered from near-war conditions in Jammu, floods and the GST cut from 12% to 5% [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). H2 domestic grew 12.72% YoY [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). Our read [AI]: domestic growth has run around 9-13% for two years [MC] (CALL Jun 2025; CALL Jul 2026), which looks like the organic run-rate.

**New lines.** Management quantified 3D resins +40.5%, printers +162% and Oradox -2% [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). Their absolute size is not disclosed. Our read [AI]: on FY25 bases of about Rs 0.5 cr for resins and Oradox [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), these lines added well under Rs 1 cr of revenue.

blocks.text: Order-driven versus organic [AI]: the business is overwhelmingly organic and repeat-purchase, through dealer reorders. The order-driven elements are export distributor shipments, OEM/private-label contracts and the occasional large consignment, such as the planned Dubai shipment that did not happen because of the war [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). Their share of revenue is not disclosed.

blocks.text: Q1 FY27 (Jun 2026) revenue was Rs 19.07 cr, up 20.9% YoY and 0.7% QoQ, and PAT was Rs 5.64 cr [F] (NUMBERS). TTM sales are Rs 75 cr [F] (NUMBERS). The company has not disclosed any order backlog or deferred orders. The only deferred item management mentioned is a Dubai consignment for Oradox, delayed by the war, which it expects to 'compensate this year' [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). Management gave no FY27 revenue or margin guidance on the June 2026 call. The standing medium-term statement is to cross Rs 100 cr within three years [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

blocks.text: The rupee amounts apply the percentages to consolidated revenue of Rs 71.81 cr. The annual report does not state the basis [E]. Country-level data and multi-year regional history are not disclosed. Net foreign exchange earnings were Rs 39.05 cr against outgo of Rs 14.98 cr in FY26, compared with Rs 35.87 cr and Rs 13.02 cr in FY25 [F] (AR2026 p.47).

North America is 1.77% of FY26 revenue [F] (AR2026 p.9). In H1 FY25 the MD said North America was about 3% of revenue [MC] (CALL Nov 2024), and management has since claimed US growth of 43-47% in H1 FY26 and 37.58% in FY26 [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Jul 2026). Those claims are hard to square with a falling share. We do not reconcile them.

The export share rose from about 55.9% to 57.9% in FY26 [E] (AR2026 p.80). That reflects domestic disruption in H1 and an export rebound [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), not a change in strategy [AI]. In Jun 2025 the CMO said the company had decided to 'intensify the focus on the domestic market' [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), and the MD described both markets as priorities [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Strategy and outcome do not line up neatly.

items: **Currency.** Exports bring in more foreign currency than imports use, so the company is naturally net long on foreign currency [E] (AR2026 p.47). FX gains were Rs 0.49 cr in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.80). Hedging policy and the currency mix are not disclosed.
**Customer-country forex crises.** These have been a recurring headwind in some African and Asian markets [MC] (CALL Nov 2024; CALL Jun 2025).

**US tariffs.** In Nov 2025 management said tariffs had some impact and that prices were realigned with buyers absorbing part [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Tariff rates and dates are not disclosed in our documents. The US is about 1.8% of revenue [F] (AR2026 p.9), so direct exposure is small [AI].
**Middle East conflict.** It delayed the UAE subsidiary's start and a Dubai consignment around March 2026, and disrupted Q4 FY26 shipping [MC] (CALL Jul 2026).
**Domestic GST.** The GST rate on products fell from 12% to 5% in Aug-Sep 2025, causing 15-20 days of channel disruption [MC] (CALL Nov 2025; CALL Jul 2026).

blocks.text: All production is at one facility in Samba district, Jammu & Kashmir [F] (AR2026 p.19). In Q1 FY26 operations stopped for about 10 days during 'a near war-like situation in Jammu' and for another 10-15 days because of floods [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Insurance expense more than doubled from Rs 0.19 cr to Rs 0.43 cr [F] (AR2026 p.81), but the disclosures do not show coverage levels or business-interruption cover. We treat this as a structural risk that the multiple does not reflect [AI].

subsections.title: Case studies, agreements and our read

blocks.text: **Case studies.** The only disclosed case study is the Oradox pharma pilot in one state: about 200 pharmacies and 250 prescribing doctors within roughly six months of starting in April-May 2024 [MC] (CALL Nov 2024). Its revenue was not given. Oradox revenue has not scaled since: about Rs 0.5 cr in FY25 and -2% in FY26 [MC] (CALL Jun 2025; CALL Jul 2026).

**Long-term agreements versus purchase orders.** The company says it has no long-term contracts [F] (AR2026 p.92). Some chains have a 'definite arrangement' for selected products [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Everything else appears to be purchase-order or dealer reorder business [AI].

**Is concentration improving or worsening?** It cannot be determined from the disclosures. The dealer count rose on management's figures [MC] (CALL Jun 2025; PPT Jul 2026). Two readings fit the data [AI]. On the optimistic reading, end demand is fragmented across thousands of dentists, so concentration risk is low. On the sceptical reading, the dealer layer (145 dealers in India, 120 overseas partners) is the real counterparty and could be concentrated without investors knowing. subsections.title: Utilisation trend and why it changed

blocks.text: Management's utilisation figures do not form a consistent series. In Nov 2024 it said 45-50% on one 8-hour shift [MC] (CALL Nov 2024). In Jun 2026 it said 67-68% of traditional installed capacity [MC] (CALL Jul 2026). Between those dates sales grew from Rs 63 cr (FY25) to Rs 72 cr (FY26), about 14% [F] (NUMBERS). A roughly 40% rise in utilisation on 14% more revenue only fits if capacity was redefined, the mix shifted to heavier products, or inventory was built ahead of sales [AI]. Inventory did rise 35.6% [E] (AR2026 p.77).

Management's arithmetic does not tie. If 67-68% utilisation corresponds to about Rs 72 cr of revenue, full capacity would be about Rs 106 cr [E]. Management says Rs 125 cr [MC] (CALL Jul 2026), which implies about 57% current utilisation [E]. These figures are not reconciled.

But the gross margin proxy slipped from 78.3% to 76.9% [E] (AR2026 p.85), and material consumed grew about twice as fast as revenue [E] (AR2026 p.77). items: **FY25 (36% to 35%).** Management cited higher exhibition and marketing spend, and depreciation on the newly capitalised building and research centre [MC] (CALL Nov 2024). Our read [AI]: largely structural. The spending is recurring and management said it will not fall [MC] (CALL Jun 2025).

Our DCF is a five-year free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) model [F] (NUMBERS). FCFF equals EBITDA minus tax on EBIT, minus capex, minus the change in net working capital. Growth fades linearly from a starting rate to a year-5 rate, and a Gordon terminal value follows. Equity value equals EV minus borrowings. The inputs [F] (NUMBERS) are:

Discount rate: risk-free 7% and equity risk premium 7%, beta 1.15, giving a cost of equity and WACC of 15% (no debt).
Terminal growth: 5.5%.

blocks.text: Simple average: 72 / 15 = 4.8 out of 10 [E]. This is a summary of our assessments, not a rating.

Prevest is a profitable, debt-free maker of specialised dental consumables. It has a 25-year export franchise in 90+ countries, global regulatory approvals and a stable 35% operating margin [F] (NUMBERS; AR2026 p.21). Its core business earns very high returns on operating capital [E]. It has spare capacity [MC] (CALL Jul 2026), more than half its assets in cash [E] (AR2026 p.77), and promoters who own 73.6% [F] (NUMBERS). Growth re-accelerated to 20.9% in Q1 FY27 [F] (NUMBERS).

The price of Rs 377 is 2.1-3.3x the DCF fair values of Rs 114-179 [E] (NUMBERS). It requires about 37% a year sales growth [F] (NUMBERS), which neither the record, the plant nor management's own targets support. Headline numbers are flattered: EBITDA includes treasury income, and revenue claims have used total income [MC] (CALL Jul 2026; CALL Jun 2025). Growth guidance is repeatedly missed. Governance has documented lapses, and the promoter family takes about a fifth of profit as pay [F] (AR2026 p.52, p.80). The overseas expansion is unaudited and loss-making [F] (AR2026 p.96).

The price implies an outcome well beyond the bull case: a company several times its current size within five years [AI]. That would need a successful new vertical or large capex, neither of which is in the disclosures. A realistic good outcome is the bull case plus a better use of cash. A realistic bad outcome is the bear case plus a governance or single-site event [AI].

subsections.title: Where the price sits and why

blocks.text: At Rs 377 the shares trade above all three DCF fair values: 3.3x bear (Rs 114.2), 2.5x base (Rs 148.4) and 2.1x bull (Rs 179.3) [E] (NUMBERS). Three things drive the gap [AI]. First, the market is willing to pay for growth optionality in digital dentistry, OEM and the US that is not yet visible in revenue. Second, our model excludes cash and starts from a low growth rate. Third, SME-platform scarcity and a thin float keep price discovery weak. Even after allowing for the model's conservative choices, the evidence does not support the current price on fundamentals [AI]. This is a research view, not a rating or price target.
